newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar dodges election worries to hit 8-yr high.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar dodges election worries to hit 8-yr high.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar dodged concerns about next month's election to soar over 70 U.S. cents on Wednesday for the first time in over eight years.
Foreign currency experts put the Kiwi's rise down to essentially one factor -- high short-term interest rates.
"It's purely a yield-driven issue. The high-yielding New Zealand assets are attracting the retail investor in Japan and in Europe," said ANZ Bank's senior manager of foreign exchange, Bill Murdoch.

"Practically every day and night you hear stories of eurokiwis going off, people buying bonds, samurais going -- the demand is on daily basis. And that is currently against those who have shorted the currency on political concern," said Bankers Trust chief foreign exchange dealer Sean Brown.

"The election looks like a 50/50 call. You can see reasons why people would want to sell it on a political basis, but people are getting hurt because the dominant factor in the market is people chasing the yield," Brown said.

The Kiwi traded up over 70 U.S. cents for the first time since mid-1988 at noon on Wednesday. The New Zealand dollar Trade-Weighted Index (TWI), which is weighted against a basket of currencies, also hit an 8-1/2 year high of 66.74.
Murdoch said a slew of eurokiwi and dual currency samurai issues -- nearly NZ$3 billion this year, with most in the last three months -- has fuelled the Kiwi's rise.

Typically, Japanese housewives are getting 7-8 percent higher yields from their investment in New Zealand dollar assets than they would at home and it would take more than a 15 percent plunge in the New Zealand dollar -- one of the world's strongest
currencies in recent years -- for them to lose money.
"The end holder is small retail, who are either oblivious to, or prepared to ignore, the potential risks that could be in the market," said Murdoch.
The main risk is the election on October 12, with opinion polls showing three parties on the left have a realistic chance of toppling the conservative National Party government.

However, currency risks even with a change of government are assessed as relatively low. Under the new mixed member proportional electoral system, major policy shifts will be hard to engineer among multi-party governments. More importantly, the
Labour Party, likely to be at the centre of any leftist government, is committed to maintain the indpendence of the Reserve Bank Act with its goal of price stability.

"If you look at the yields and what's available in other countries around the world, and then you look at those other countries' political scene, it makes any outcome in the New Zealand October 12 election look pretty benign," said Stu Nattrass, National Bank of NZ's joint head of Treasury.
The local market and some influential U.S. investors had taken a bearish view of the currency, expecting to be able to buy it back cheaper on election jitters, he said.
"There will be some volatility, but the big sell-off that people are looking for, what sort of level is it going to be on?" he said, adding the Kiwi was now fair value to expensive.
The Reserve Bank last Friday, against many market expectations, had virtually underwritten short-term interest rates of around 10 percent at least until the year end.

The long-awaited easing of monetary screws was again postponed in the bank's six monthly economic forecasts. And even the bank's desire to change the monetary mix to a lower currency and higher interest rates, to ease pressure on the tradeable sector, is seen at best as wishful thinking.
The RB said its forecasts assumed a TWI of 65 -- that level taking account of an easing at some future unspecified date.
"Except for one-off shock factors, it would be difficult to envisage a TWI of 65 while short-dated interest rates remain near 10 percent," said Murdoch.
"I'm not saying it won't happen, but as long as there is on-going issuance of samurais or euros then there is going to be ongoing support for the currency on any dips," he said.

Brown said the higher the Kiwi goes the easier it will be to fall. "Common sense would say over the next three weeks we will get some dips in the currency... but the nature of the game is that the main driver is not the political risk but people chasing the interest rates," he said.
